common_name: Hinomayo Azalea (Historic Clear Pink Kurume Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Hinomayo is a pre-1910 Japanese Kurume azalea prized for its clear, soft pink flowers on a dense, upright plant.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil rich in organic matter, siting the shrub in partial shade such as beneath high pines or open hardwoods where filtered light reaches the foliage. Hinomayo is one of the oldest and most widely grown Kurume azaleas, predating the famous Wilson introductions of the 1910s, and is valued for its slow, dense, upright habit and its small, clear candy-pink flowers that completely blanket the plant during its heavy spring flush. Its glossy, small, olive-green leaves stay tidy and compact even without frequent shearing, making it a good choice for foundation plantings and mixed shrub borders in older Gulf South gardens. Water deeply during the first two years while roots establish, and prune only immediately after flowering, since next year's buds set on the current season's growth.
sources: American Rhododendron Society — Journal (Kurume Azaleas history)

common_name: Kure-no-Yuki Azalea (Dwarf White Kurume Azalea, Snowflake)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Kure-no-Yuki, whose name translates roughly as 'snow of Kure,' is a compact old Japanese Kurume azalea grown for its masses of white late-spring flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in a sheltered spot with partial shade, since this old Japanese cultivar is somewhat less cold-hardy than many other Kurume selections and benefits from wind protection. Kure-no-Yuki is a compact, spreading, dwarf Kurume azalea with small, leathery, glossy dark-green leaves that disappear each May beneath a heavy cover of white flowers touched with a faint greenish flare at the throat. Its low, dense habit suits it well to cascading over low walls, edging shaded beds, or massing at the front of a mixed shrub border in Gulf South landscapes. Keep soil consistently moist but never soggy, and shear lightly right after bloom to maintain its tidy mounded shape, since flower buds for next spring form on the current year's new growth.

common_name: Glory of Sunninghill Azalea (Brick Red-Orange Southern Indica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Glory of Sunninghill is a large, vigorous Southern Indica azalea grown for its showy brick red-orange spring flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade beneath high pines or open hardwoods, giving the shrub room to reach its full mature spread. Glory of Sunninghill is a big, rounded, mounding Southern Indica azalea with glossy rich-green foliage and a heavy mid-spring flush of showy, funnel-shaped, brick red-orange flowers that read as one of the warmer, more saturated colors in the Southern Indica palette. Like other Southern Indica types it tolerates deep shade better than sun-hungry deciduous azaleas, though bloom is heaviest with at least a few hours of dappled or morning light. Water deeply while establishing and during summer dry spells, and prune immediately after flowering only if needed, since buds for the next season's bloom set soon after the current flush fades.

common_name: Dorothy Gish Azalea (Frilled Red-Orange Rutherfordiana Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; Dorothy Gish is a vigorous Rutherfordiana hybrid azalea grown for its frilled, hose-in-hose, red-orange flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil, choosing a site with morning sun and afternoon shade in hot Gulf South summers to protect flower color and foliage from scorch. Dorothy Gish is a heavy-blooming Rutherfordiana hybrid azalea whose frilled, hose-in-hose, red-orange flowers with darker flares open in a mid-season flush on a large, vigorous shrub that can exceed 6 feet at maturity. It tolerates more sun than many older Indica-type azaleas but still performs best with some shade during the hottest part of the day near the Gulf Coast. Water deeply during establishment and dry spells, and prune only right after flowering, since next year's flower buds form on the current season's growth.

common_name: Kozan Azalea (Pale Pink Satsuki Bonsai Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Kozan is a compact, late-blooming Satsuki azalea popular both as a landscape dwarf and as a traditional bonsai subject.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter in partial shade, since Satsuki types bloom later than other azalea groups and appreciate protection from harsh afternoon sun. Kozan is a compact, twiggy, rounded Satsuki azalea long ranked among the most popular varieties for traditional bonsai alongside cultivars like Kinsai, prized for its pale pink to nearly white funnel-shaped flowers with a soft green throat that open in late May and June, well after most spring azaleas have finished. Its dense, low, spreading habit also suits it to foundation plantings and border edges in shaded Gulf South gardens. Keep the shallow root zone consistently moist with a layer of mulch, and shear lightly right after bloom, since Satsuki azaleas set next year's flower buds on wood produced soon after flowering ends.

common_name: Beni Kirishima Azalea (Double Reddish-Orange Kurume-Group Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Beni Kirishima is an old Japanese cultivar of the Kirishima azalea group grown for its double, reddish-orange flowers.

directions: Plant in evenly moist, well-drained, acidic soil enriched with organic matter, siting the shrub where it receives mostly sun to mostly shade with relief from the harshest afternoon summer heat. Beni Kirishima is an old Japanese azalea of the Kirishima group, closely related to the Kurume azaleas bred in Kurume City, and is grown for its dense clusters of double, funnel-shaped, reddish-orange flowers that open in late May, later than most Kurume cultivars. Its evergreen foliage and dense branching make it useful as a mid-height accent or informal hedge in a partly shaded shrub border. Water regularly through the growing season, especially in the first year, and prune right after flowering, since flower buds for the following year form on new growth soon after bloom.

common_name: Fisher Pink Azalea (Single Pink Southern Indica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Fisher Pink is a Southern Indica azalea grown for its abundant clusters of single, clear pink, three-inch flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade beneath high pines or open hardwoods typical of older Gulf Coast gardens. Fisher Pink is a Southern Indica azalea that produces heavy clusters of single, clear pink flowers roughly three inches across in a dramatic mid-spring flush, on a large evergreen shrub that provides dense year-round structure in a mixed border or as a woodland-edge planting. It tolerates deep shade better than sun-loving shrubs but blooms most heavily with some filtered morning light. Water deeply during establishment and dry summer stretches, and prune only immediately after flowering if shaping is needed, since next year's buds form soon after the current bloom fades.

common_name: Iveryana Azalea (Dwarf White Pink-Flecked Southern Indica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Iveryana is a heirloom dwarf Southern Indica azalea whose white flowers are randomly flecked and striped with pink to red.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, since this heirloom dwarf tolerates low light better than most flowering shrubs. Iveryana forms a mounding, medium-textured evergreen shrub bearing showy, trumpet-shaped white flowers two to three inches across, each randomly flecked and striped with pink to red in a pattern that varies from bush to bush and even bloom to bloom, giving established plantings a lively, painterly look during the late-spring flush. Its smaller mature size compared with many Southern Indica cultivars makes it a good fit for foundation plantings or as an understory accent beneath high pines and oaks. Water deeply while establishing and prune only right after flowering, since flower buds for the next season set on the current year's growth.

common_name: Pride of Dorking Azalea (Deep Fuchsia-Red Southern Indica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Pride of Dorking is a fast-growing, sun-tolerant Southern Indica azalea grown for its deep fuchsia-red trumpet flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, though this vigorous selection tolerates more sun than many older Southern Indica cultivars. Pride of Dorking is a dense, rounded, fast-growing shrub with leathery, slightly glaucous evergreen foliage and a heavy mid-spring flush of showy, deep fuchsia-red, trumpet-shaped flowers that stand out strongly against the dark leaves. Its naturally attractive, well-branched form works well as a specimen shrub or in mass plantings along a shaded border. Water deeply during the first couple of growing seasons and in dry summer spells, and prune immediately after flowering only if needed, since flower buds for the following year form on new growth produced soon after bloom.

common_name: Duchess of Cypress Azalea (White Salmon-Blushed Southern Indica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in morning sun with afternoon shade or filtered light; Duchess of Cypress is a semi-dwarf branch sport of Duc de Rohan with white, salmon-blushed flowers.

directions: Plant in loam, clay, or silt soil that is moist, well-drained, and acidic, choosing a spot with morning sun and afternoon shade or dappled light beneath oaks or pines. Duchess of Cypress arose as a branch sport of the antique Southern Indica cultivar Duc de Rohan and shares its parent's vigor and antique charm, but its soft, frilly, trumpet-shaped flowers are white with a salmon-pink blush and deeper pink speckling concentrated on one side of each bloom, and its habit is somewhat more compact and semi-dwarf. It is a multi-season bloomer, with its heaviest flush in spring and scattered rebloom through the growing season. Water deeply while the shrub establishes and during dry spells, and prune right after the main spring bloom, since next year's flower buds set on the current season's new growth.
